blocks.text: A hydraulic press controller tracks its pressure setpoint beautifully in simulation. In service, the pump wears and its gain drifts upward by 40% over a year, and one morning the pressure begins to oscillate violently. The designer's mistake was not the nominal design but the lack of a number saying how much gain drift the loop could tolerate. Gain margin, phase margin and the sensitivity function supply exactly that.

blocks.markdown: Take the open-loop transfer function $L(j\omega)=G(j\omega)C(j\omega)$ of a loop that is stable and whose Nyquist plot passes the critical point $-1$ at some distance. Two frequencies on the Bode plot matter. The **gain crossover frequency** $\omega_{gc}$ is where $|L(j\omega)|=1$ (0 dB, with dB $=20\log_{10}$ of magnitude). The **phase crossover frequency** $\omega_{pc}$ is where $\angle L(j\omega)=-180^\circ$.

blocks.title: Gain margin and phase margin
blocks.text: Phase margin: $\mathrm{PM}=180^\circ+\angle L(j\omega_{gc})$, the extra phase lag the loop could take at $\omega_{gc}$ before the plot reaches $-1$. Gain margin: $\mathrm{GM}=1/|L(j\omega_{pc})|$, the factor by which the loop gain could be multiplied before the plot reaches $-1$; in decibels $\mathrm{GM}_{dB}=-20\log_{10}|L(j\omega_{pc})|$. Both must be positive (GM above 1, PM above $0^\circ$) for a loop that is stable and has the usual shape.

blocks.caption: Margins read from the Bode plot (magnitude 0 dB crossing and $-180^\circ$ phase crossing).

blocks.title: Margins of a third-order loop
blocks.prompt: For $L(s)=\dfrac{5}{s(s+1)(s+4)}$ (units: rad/s) find the phase crossover frequency, gain margin and phase margin.

steps.text: Phase crossover: expand the denominator at $s=j\omega$: $j\omega(j\omega+1)(j\omega+4)=-5\omega^2+j(4\omega-\omega^3)$. The phase is $-180^\circ$ when the imaginary part is zero (and the real part is negative).
At $\omega_{pc}$ the real part is $-5(4)=-20$, so $L(j2)=-K/20$.
Gain crossover: solve $|L(j\omega)|=1$ numerically (the magnitude falls monotonically). The solution is

blocks.answer: $\omega_{pc}=2$ rad/s, GM = 4 (12.0 dB), PM about 35 degrees at $\omega_{gc}\approx0.90$ rad/s.

blocks.markdown: **Sensitivity.** The sensitivity function $S(s)=1/(1+L(s))$ is the transfer function from an output disturbance to the output, and from the reference to the tracking error. At frequency $\omega$, $|S(j\omega)|<1$ means feedback attenuates disturbances there; $|S|>1$ means feedback amplifies them. The distance of the Nyquist plot from $-1$ at that frequency is $|1+L(j\omega)|=1/|S(j\omega)|$.

blocks.title: Evaluating S at one frequency
blocks.prompt: At a frequency of 3 rad/s the open-loop frequency response of a loop is $L=2.5\angle-150^\circ$. Find $S=1/(1+L)$ and interpret it.

steps.text: Invert to get the sensitivity magnitude; the phase is the negative of the phase of $1+L$.
Since $|S|<1$, feedback reduces a disturbance at this frequency to about 58% of its open-loop size.

blocks.answer: $|S|\approx0.585$ (about -4.7 dB): disturbances at 3 rad/s are attenuated.

blocks.caption: Margins implied by a given peak sensitivity.

blocks.markdown: The reasoning is geometric: $M_s$ is the reciprocal of the smallest distance from the Nyquist plot to $-1$. A plot that stays at least $1/M_s$ away from $-1$ cannot approach the critical point closely along the real axis (giving the GM bound) or along the unit circle (giving the PM bound). A good design has $M_s$ below roughly 1.5 to 2, GM above about 2 (6 dB) and PM between $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$.

blocks.title: Allowable plant-gain variation
blocks.prompt: A loop has a gain margin of 7.5 dB. A pump's gain is expected to vary between 0.7 and 2.0 times the design value. Is the loop guaranteed stable across this range if only the gain changes?

steps.text: Convert the margin to a factor.
Compare with the largest expected gain ratio of 2.0. An increase by any factor below GM keeps the plot from reaching $-1$ (for a loop of the usual shape).
A decrease to 0.7 of nominal only shrinks the plot toward the origin, and does not move the crossing past $-1$ for this type of loop, so it cannot destabilise it.

blocks.answer: Yes: the gain can rise by a factor of up to 2.37 before instability, comfortably above 2.0. (A margin of safety remains of about 1.19 times.)

blocks.title: Delay margin
blocks.text: A phase margin $\mathrm{PM}$ (in radians) at gain crossover $\omega_{gc}$ tolerates an extra pure time delay of $\tau_{max}=\mathrm{PM}/\omega_{gc}$ before instability, because a delay $\tau$ adds phase lag $\omega_{gc}\tau$ at that frequency without changing the magnitude. This links margins to real hardware effects such as sampling and computation delay.

blocks.title: One margin is not enough
blocks.text: A loop can have a large gain margin but a poor phase margin (or the reverse), and neither captures a plot that passes close to $-1$ at an intermediate frequency. The peak sensitivity $M_s$ checks the whole curve; report GM, PM and $M_s$ together.

points: Phase margin is $180^\circ+\angle L(j\omega_{gc})$ at the 0 dB crossing; gain margin is $1/|L(j\omega_{pc})|$ at the $-180^\circ$ crossing, in dB $=-20\log_{10}|L(j\omega_{pc})|$.
The sensitivity $S=1/(1+L)$ at a frequency measures how disturbances are attenuated ($|S|<1$) or amplified ($|S|>1$); its peak $M_s$ bounds GM and PM from below.
The gain margin gives the factor by which plant gain can rise before instability, and PM$/\omega_{gc}$ gives the tolerable extra time delay.

questions.stem: The phase margin of a stable loop is defined as

options.text: $180^\circ$ plus the phase of $L(j\omega)$ at the gain crossover frequency
$180^\circ$ plus the phase of $L(j\omega)$ at the phase crossover frequency
The magnitude of $L$ at the gain crossover frequency, in degrees
The reciprocal of the magnitude of $L$ at the phase crossover

questions.correctOptionText: $180^\circ$ plus the phase of $L(j\omega)$ at the gain crossover frequency

distractorRationale.a: At the 0 dB frequency the margin is the remaining lag before $-180^\circ$.
distractorRationale.b: At the phase crossover the phase is already $-180^\circ$, giving zero.
distractorRationale.c: The magnitude at the gain crossover is 1 by definition and is not an angle.
distractorRationale.d: This is the gain margin, not the phase margin.

questions.explanation: The phase margin is evaluated where $|L|=1$ and equals the phase there minus $-180^\circ$, i.e. $180^\circ+\angle L$. The reciprocal of the magnitude at the $-180^\circ$ frequency is the gain margin.

questions.stem: At which frequency is the gain margin read from a Bode plot?

options.text: At the lowest frequency of the plot

distractorRationale.a: This is where the phase margin is read.
distractorRationale.b: The margin is the distance of the magnitude from 0 dB at that frequency.
distractorRationale.c: The low-frequency gain tells about steady-state error, not margins.
distractorRationale.d: There is no special significance for the margin at $-90^\circ$.

questions.explanation: The gain margin asks how much more gain would put the magnitude at 0 dB at the frequency where the phase is $-180^\circ$. It is therefore read at the phase crossover, not the gain crossover.

questions.stem: A Bode plot shows $|L|=0$ dB at $\omega=4$ rad/s where the phase is $-135^\circ$. What is the phase margin?

distractorRationale.a: This forgets to add $180^\circ$ to the negative phase.
distractorRationale.b: The sign is wrong: the loop still has positive margin before $-180^\circ$.
distractorRationale.d: This subtracts the phase from $90^\circ$ instead of using $180^\circ$.

questions.explanation: PM $=180^\circ+(-135^\circ)=45^\circ$ at the frequency where the magnitude crosses 0 dB. A positive value means the loop is stable with $45^\circ$ of spare lag.

questions.stem: Where $|S(j\omega)|>1$, what does the feedback loop do to a disturbance at that frequency?

options.text: It leaves the disturbance exactly unchanged at every frequency
It amplifies the disturbance compared with the open-loop case

questions.correctOptionText: It amplifies the disturbance compared with the open-loop case

distractorRationale.b: Unchanged means $|S|=1$ and applies only if $L=0$.
distractorRationale.c: Amplification at some frequencies is normal and unavoidable; instability is a separate matter.
distractorRationale.d: $S=1/(1+L)$ is the factor by which feedback changes the disturbance effect.

questions.explanation: The sensitivity gives the ratio of the closed-loop to the open-loop effect of an output disturbance, so values above 1 mean amplification. A peak above 1 is unavoidable in practice near the crossover region.

questions.stem: True or false: a gain margin of 6 dB means the loop gain can be multiplied by about 2 before the plot reaches $-1$.
questions.explanation: $20\log_{10}2=6.02$ dB, so a 6 dB margin corresponds to a factor of about 2. Once the gain is multiplied by this factor the magnitude at the phase crossover reaches 1.

questions.stem: At the phase crossover frequency a loop has $|L(j\omega_{pc})|=0.25$. Find the gain margin in dB.
questions.explanation: The gain margin is $1/0.25=4$, which in decibels is $20\log_{10}4=12.04$ dB. The loop gain can rise four-fold before the plot reaches $-1$.

questions.stem: At one frequency a loop has $L=1.5\angle-120^\circ$. Find the magnitude of the sensitivity $|S|=|1/(1+L)|$ (dimensionless).
A design requires peak sensitivity no larger than $M_s=1.6$. Using $\mathrm{GM}\ge M_s/(M_s-1)$, find the minimum gain margin guaranteed, in dB.
questions.explanation: $M_s/(M_s-1)=1.6/0.6=2.667$, and $20\log_{10}2.667=8.52$ dB. So any loop with $M_s\le1.6$ can tolerate at least a factor 2.67 gain increase.

questions.stem: A loop has a phase margin of $40^\circ$ at a gain crossover frequency of 5 rad/s. (i) Explain the physical meaning of the phase margin. (ii) Estimate the largest additional pure time delay the loop can tolerate. (iii) Explain why a gain margin alone would not reveal this.
markingGuide: Phase margin is the additional phase lag at $\omega_{gc}$ that would put the plot through $-1$ (instability).
A delay $\tau$ adds lag $\omega_{gc}\tau$ rad, so $\tau_{max}=\mathrm{PM}/\omega_{gc}=(40\pi/180)/5\approx0.14$ s.
Delay changes only phase, not magnitude, so it erodes the phase margin and not the gain margin.
Gain margin is measured at a different frequency, so a large GM can coexist with a small PM and little delay tolerance.
questions.explanation: The phase margin is the extra lag at gain crossover that would drive the loop unstable. A delay $\tau$ adds $\omega_{gc}\tau$ radians of lag, so the tolerable delay is $(40\pi/180)/5\approx0.14$ s; this is a phase effect and is not indicated by the gain margin, which is read at another frequency.

questions.stem: A pressure loop has a gain margin of 3 dB and a phase margin of $50^\circ$. The plant gain is known to drift upward by up to 40%. Decide whether the design is acceptable and justify your answer using the peak sensitivity bound $M_s\ge \mathrm{GM}/(\mathrm{GM}-1)$.
markingGuide: Notes a 40% increase (factor 1.4) is just below 1.41, so stability is barely retained with essentially no safety margin.
Computes $M_s\ge1.41/0.41\approx3.4$, a very large peak showing poor robustness near $-1$.
Concludes the design is unacceptable and suggests reducing loop gain or adding lead compensation, targeting GM of at least 6 dB and $M_s$ near 2 or lower.
questions.explanation: A gain margin of 3 dB is a factor of 1.41, so a 40% gain increase leaves almost no allowance. The bound gives $M_s\ge1.41/0.41\approx3.4$, indicating the plot comes dangerously close to $-1$; the loop gain should be reduced or the loop reshaped to obtain at least 6 dB of margin.
